newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan sees Indian threat to security and talks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan sees Indian threat to security and talks.

text.p: Pakistan said on Wednesday India's missile development was a threat to regional security and recent killings of militant leaders in disputed Kashmir could damage this month's peace talks between the two nations.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman said development and deployment of short- and medium-range missiles by India, Pakistan's arch-rival, "directly affects regional security".

"It is incumbent upon the international community to impress upon India the desirability of avoiding a new arms race in South Asia," he said in comments on New Delhi's plans to launch a new medium-range surface-to-air missile next year.

An Indian Defence Ministry scientific adviser, Abdul Kalam, said on Monday trials of short-range, surface-to-surface Prithvi missiles had been completed and that the surface-to-air Akash missile would be ready for launch next year.

The Pakistani spokesman also said last week's killings of four separatist militant leaders by Indian security forces in Kashmir would vitiate the atmosphere for a resumption of stalled peace talks between foreign ministry secretaries of the two countries set for March 28-31.

India says the four guerrillas of the pro-Pakistan Hizb-ul-Mujahideen group were killed in shootouts with paramilitary soldiers. But Hizb and Pakistani officials say the guerrillas were killed while in Indian custody.
"Such infensible actions would only vitiate the atmosphere for the forthcoming foreign secretary-level talks," the Pakistani spokesman said.

He accused India of "massive repression" in the two-thirds of Kashmir it rules and said this policy had "failed to deter the Kashmiri people who were resolved to continue their struggle to achieve their right to self-determination".
Pakistan controls the remainder of the Himalayan region, over which the countries have fought two of their three wars since independence from Britain in 1947.

The dates for the talks, after a deadlock of more than three years, were set for March 28-31 following an exchange of conciliatory messages last month between Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and his new Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif.
The last such talks were held in January 1994 but became bogged down over differences on Kashmir.
Foreign Ministers Inder Kumar Gujar of India and Gohar Ayub of Pakistan are also due to meet in New Delhi on the sidelines of a non-aligned foreign ministers' meeting there on April 7-8.
India, which is fighting a separatist Moslem revolt in its part of Kashmir, says the whole region is its integral part.

But Islamabad, which denies New Delhi's charges of training and arming the separatists, wants the mainly Moslem Kashmiris to be allowed to vote in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
